title: Mental Disorders and their Treatment
summary: Mental disorders develop gradually from heredity, personality weaknesses, low stress tolerance, childhood experiences, stressful situations and inability to cope. Situations perceived as difficult to cope with are stressors. Hans Selye coined 'stress' and defined it as a non-specific response of the body to any demand on it (a physiological basis: hormones of the adrenal and other glands). Two categories: eustress (moderate, desirable stress, e.g. playing a competitive sport) and distress (bad, excessive, irrational stress). The recent approach stresses appraisal of the situation in relation to the coping resources; adaptation is the process by which people manage the environment to maintain optimum physical, psychological and social well-being.

Stressors: major life events and changes (marriage, retirement, divorce); daily hassles (misplacing things, deadlines, traffic jams, waiting in lines); chronic role strain (difficult marriage, disabled child, poverty); traumas (nuclear attack, bomb blast, death of a loved one). Responses: behavioural (alcohol or drug abuse, sleep disturbance, restlessness, aggression, irritability, withdrawal), emotional (anxiety, depression, anger, guilt, shame), cognitive (negative self-concept, pessimism, cognitive distortion), interpersonal (passive or aggressive relationships, competitiveness, isolation), biological (high blood pressure, diabetes, flu, lowered immunity, fatigue) and imagery (helplessness, failure, losing control).

Stress arises when obstacles block goals. Approach–approach conflict: choosing between two desirable goals (two invitations on the same evening). Avoidance–avoidance conflict: choosing between two undesirable goals, 'caught between the devil and the deep blue sea' (unemployment versus a low-paid disagreeable job); resolution may bring frustration. Approach–avoidance conflict: strong tendency both to approach and avoid the same goal (wants to marry for security but fears loss of freedom); 'mixed-blessing'; resolved by accepting positive and negative features. Frustration is an experiential state from blocking of needs and motives by external forces or from absence of a desired goal; hindrances are physical or social (accidents, unhealthy relationships, death of a loved one) or personal (handicap, inadequate competence, lack of self-discipline); delay, lack of resources, failure, loss and loneliness.

Coping may be problem-focused (intellectual resources), emotion-focused (crying) or defence-oriented (justifying own actions); repeated defence-oriented coping can lead to disorders. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM) of the American Psychiatric Association lists disorders; abnormal psychology studies them. (A) Childhood disorders: ADHD (attention problems, over-activity) and autistic disorder (withdrawn, does not smile, delayed language). (B) Anxiety disorders: phobia (extreme irrational fear) and obsessive-compulsive disorder (repetitive thoughts or actions). (C) Mood disorders: depression (sadness, loss of interest, sleep and appetite disturbance, lethargy, guilt, worthlessness, hopelessness, poor concentration; at least two weeks needs clinical intervention) and bipolar disorder (alternating depression and mania). (D) Psychosomatic disorders (physical symptoms with psychological causes: blood pressure, diabetes, hypertension) and somatoform disorders (physical symptoms without identifiable biological cause, e.g. stomach pain with no organ problem). (E) Dissociative disorders: dissociative amnesia, dissociative fugue (memory loss plus new identity), depersonalization disorder and multiple personality (dissociative identity) disorder. (F) Schizophrenia: disturbances of thought, emotion and behaviour: incoherent thinking, faulty perception, disturbed motor activity, flat or inappropriate emotions, withdrawal into delusions (false beliefs) and hallucinations (false sensory perceptions); a type is catatonic schizophrenia. (G) Personality disorders: inflexible, maladaptive patterns rooted in early childhood, in three clusters – odd or eccentric (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal), anxious and apprehensive (avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive) and dramatic, emotional or erratic (antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic).

A clinical psychologist or psychotherapist treats a client; psychotherapy is called the 'talking cure' (interpersonal contact); medicines are given only by a psychiatrist, a medical doctor specialised in mental disorders. Approaches: psychoanalysis, behaviour therapy, cognitive-behaviour therapy and client-centred therapy. Steps: (i) rapport formation, (ii) preparation of case history, (iii) determination of the problem (clinical tests and interview), (iv) therapeutic sessions (progress monitored), (v) termination of therapeutic intervention.

Task-oriented coping is a conscious, rational, constructive action with three forms: attack (confront the situation, choose the best course, stay flexible, develop new resources, e.g. a student plans revision), withdrawal (admit defeat, leave the situation or redirect effort to a more appropriate goal, e.g. making friends elsewhere) and compromise (accept a substitute goal, lower level of aspiration). Defence-oriented (emotion-focused) coping makes one feel comfortable without a solution: rationalisation (all students failed since the paper was tough) and displacement (scolding a younger brother for anger at a strict teacher). A healthy life-style with positive thinking, emotions and actions best copes with stress.

objective: Define stress according to Hans Selye.
A non-specific response of the body to any demand on it.
Name the two categories of stress.
Name the four categories of stressors.
Major life events and changes, daily hassles, chronic role strain and traumas.
Name the three types of conflict.
An experiential state resulting from blocking of needs and motives by external forces or the absence of a desired goal.
Differentiate psychosomatic and somatoform disorders in one line.
Psychosomatic: physical symptoms with psychological causes; somatoform: physical symptoms with no identifiable biological cause.
Dissociative amnesia, dissociative fugue, depersonalization disorder, multiple personality disorder (any two).
objective4: Identify the stressor category: (i) divorce; (ii) misplacing items; (iii) living in poverty; (iv) death of a loved one.
(i) Major life event. (ii) Daily hassle. (iii) Chronic role strain. (iv) Trauma.

Name the conflict: (i) two desirable invitations on the same night; (ii) unemployment or a disagreeable job; (iii) wanting to marry but fearing responsibilities; (iv) which is called a mixed-blessing conflict?
Name the coping type: (i) planning revision for a tough test; (ii) leaving a rejecting friend and making a new one; (iii) accepting a substitute goal; (iv) blaming a tough paper for failure.
Write the steps of psychotherapy in order (first four).
Rapport formation; preparation of case history; determination of the problem; therapeutic sessions (then termination).
vsa: Differentiate eustress and distress with examples.
Eustress is moderate desirable stress such as playing a competitive sport; distress is excessive, undesirable stress.
What are daily hassles? Give two examples.
Irritating, frustrating demands of everyday life such as deadlines and traffic jams.
A strong tendency both to approach and to avoid the same goal, e.g. wanting to marry yet fearing loss of freedom.
Attention-deficit hyperactive disorder: a childhood disorder with difficulty paying attention and extreme over-activity.
A mental state of sadness, loss of interest, sleep and appetite disturbance, guilt and hopelessness lasting at least two weeks.
A serious dissociative disorder in which several distinct personalities emerge in the same person at different times.
A medical doctor specialised in mental disorders who can prescribe medicines.
sa: Explain the recent approach to stress.
It focuses on appraisal of a situation in relation to the person's coping resources; appraisal and coping determine adaptation, the management of the environment to maintain well-being.
Major life events (marriage, retirement), daily hassles (deadlines), chronic role strain (difficult marriage, poverty) and traumas (bomb blast, death of a loved one).
Explain the types of conflict with examples.
Approach–approach between two desirable goals; avoidance–avoidance between two undesirable goals; approach–avoidance with attraction and fear of the same goal.
A disorder of thought, emotion and behaviour: incoherent thinking, faulty perception, disturbed movement, flat or inappropriate emotions and withdrawal into delusions and hallucinations.
Rapport formation, case history, determination of the problem, therapeutic sessions with progress monitoring and termination of intervention with follow-up advice.
Task-oriented coping is rational and constructive (attack, withdrawal, compromise); defence-oriented coping makes one feel comfortable without solving the problem (rationalisation, displacement).
la: Define stress and discuss the stressors and responses to them.

Stress is a non-specific response of the body to demands (Selye): eustress and distress. Stressors: major life events, daily hassles, chronic role strain and traumas. Responses: behavioural, emotional, cognitive, interpersonal, biological and imagery.
Explain how conflict and frustration lead to stress.

Obstacles to goals cause conflict (approach–approach, avoidance–avoidance, approach–avoidance) and frustration from blocked needs or absent goals, caused by physical and social hindrances and personal limits; their intensity makes them stressful.
Describe any five mental disorders and their symptoms.

Anxiety (phobia, OCD), mood (depression, bipolar), psychosomatic and somatoform, dissociative (amnesia, fugue, depersonalization, multiple personality), schizophrenia (delusions, hallucinations), childhood (ADHD, autism) and personality disorders in three clusters.
Discuss the psychotherapeutic process and the desirable ways of coping with stress.

Psychotherapy by a clinical psychologist follows rapport, case history, problem identification, sessions and termination; approaches include psychoanalysis, behaviour, cognitive-behaviour and client-centred therapy. Coping: attack, withdrawal and compromise, avoiding defence mechanisms, with a healthy life-style and positive thinking.
